examples: literally 'age is the same as me'
The prices are all the same.
nuance: 같다 means two or more things match or are identical. To say 'the same as N', use N하고/N과 같다. Note that 같이 (together/like) and N 같아요 (seems like N) come from the same root but have different meanings, so context matters.
mistakes: Saying '같다 같다' to mean 'similar' — for 'similar but not identical' use 비슷하다, not 같다.
Forgetting the particle: say 'A하고 B가 같아요', not just 'A B 같아요'.

examples: The taste is a bit different.
Do you have another color too?
nuance: 다르다 is the opposite of 같다 and conjugates as 르 irregular: 다르 + 아요 becomes 달라요. The pre-noun form 다른 is extremely common and means both 'different' and 'another'. Don't confuse 다르다 (different) with 틀리다 (wrong); they are often mixed up even by native speakers.
mistakes: Using 틀리다 ('to be wrong') when you mean 'different' — they are not the same in standard Korean.
Saying '다라요' instead of the correct 르-irregular form '달라요'.

english: to be exactly the same / identical
examples: It's exactly the same as this one.
Give me exactly the same one too.
nuance: 똑같다 is a stronger, more emphatic version of 같다, stressing that things are identical with no difference at all. It's very common in everyday speech. The adverb 똑같이 means 'identically / in the same way' and is useful when ordering or copying something.
mistakes: Using 똑같다 when things are merely similar — for 'kind of alike' use a softer word.
Dropping the particle: say '저거하고 똑같아요', not '저거 똑같아요'.

nuance: 아름답다 is the proper word for 'beautiful', used most often for scenery, nature, music, or moments rather than everyday cuteness. It's a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so it becomes 아름다워요. For people, especially women, 예쁘다 is more common in casual speech, while 아름답다 sounds a bit more formal or poetic.
mistakes: Saying '아름답어요' — the ㅂ irregular gives '아름다워요'.
Overusing 아름답다 for food or small cute things; 예쁘다 or 맛있다 fits better there.

nuance: 훌륭하다 expresses high praise for quality, ability, or character — 'excellent, admirable, fine'. It's a notch more formal and weighty than 좋다 ('good'), so it works well for complimenting someone's work, skill, or a person's character. You'll hear it in reviews, school, and polite compliments.
mistakes: Using 훌륭하다 for casual 'nice/good' situations where 좋다 is enough — it can sound overly grand.
Mixing up the adjective form: it's 훌륭한 N, not 훌륭하는 N (adjectives use -ㄴ/은, not -는).

examples: You did it all alone? Amazing!
nuance: 대단하다 is a go-to compliment meaning 'impressive, amazing, remarkable', often aimed at a person's achievement or ability. It's warmer and more spoken than 훌륭하다, perfect for reacting to something someone did. With a flat tone it can also describe something as 'considerable/serious' (대단한 일 = a big deal).
mistakes: Saying 대단하다 about your own success — it sounds boastful; use it to praise others.
Confusing it with 대단히 (an adverb meaning 'very/greatly'), which modifies other words.

examples: The taste is kind of ordinary.
nuance: 평범하다 means 'ordinary, average, nothing special' and is neutral — not an insult. It's the natural opposite of 특별하다 ('special'). Koreans often use it modestly to describe themselves or everyday routines. Tone decides whether it sounds humble or slightly disappointed.
mistakes: Treating 평범하다 as fully negative; it usually just means 'normal/unremarkable'.
Using the pre-noun form wrong: it's 평범한 사람, not 평범하는 사람.

examples: It's a common thing around here.
This kind of color isn't common.
nuance: 흔하다 means something is common, easily found, or seen everywhere. Its opposite is 드물다 ('rare'). Saying something is 흔하다 can be neutral ('widely available') or slightly negative ('too common, unoriginal'), so tone matters. It's handy for talking about prices, names, items, and situations.
mistakes: Confusing 흔하다 (common) with 흔들다 (to shake) — different words, similar look.
Using 흔하다 for people's personality; for 'an ordinary person' use 평범하다 instead.

nuance: 소중하다 describes something dear, treasured, and emotionally valuable — people, time, memories, gifts. It's about worth to your heart, not price in money (for expensive use 비싸다). It carries warm feeling, so it's a lovely word for cards, messages, and heartfelt moments.
mistakes: Using 소중하다 for monetary cost; for 'expensive' say 비싸다.
Saying 소중하는 N for the pre-noun form; adjectives take -ㄴ, so it's 소중한 N.

examples: I'm used to the work now.
에 marks what you're used to
nuance: 익숙하다 means 'familiar / accustomed to', describing something you've done or seen enough that it feels easy and natural. The thing you're used to takes the particle 에: 운전에 익숙해요 ('I'm used to driving'). Its opposite is 낯설다 ('unfamiliar'). Very useful for talking about settling into a new life.
mistakes: Marking the object with 을/를 instead of 에 — say '한국에 익숙해요', not '한국을 익숙해요'.
Confusing 익숙하다 (familiar) with 익다 (to ripen/be cooked).

examples: Please give me a clear answer.
nuance: 분명하다 means something is clear, definite, and not vague — used for reasons, answers, facts, and intentions. The adverb form 분명히 ('clearly / surely / definitely') is even more common in speech, often expressing the speaker's certainty. It overlaps with 확실하다, but 분명하다 leans toward 'unambiguous/obvious'.
mistakes: Confusing 분명하다 with visual clarity; for a clear photo or sound use 선명하다.
Forgetting that the adverb is 분명히, not 분명하게 in most everyday speech.

nuance: 확실하다 expresses certainty and confidence — you're sure something is true or settled. The adverb 확실히 ('certainly, definitely, for sure') is common when answering or confirming. It's close to 분명하다, but 확실하다 focuses on the speaker's confidence/sureness, while 분명하다 stresses that something is obvious.
mistakes: Saying 확실하다 when you actually mean 'maybe' — for uncertainty use 아마 ('probably').
Writing the adverb as 확실하게 in casual speech; 확실히 is the natural choice.

usage: it's possible / it can be done
nuance: 가능하다 means 'possible / doable / available' and is super practical for daily questions — '예약 가능해요?' ('Is a reservation possible?'). It often replaces a longer '-ㄹ 수 있다' sentence in shops and service settings. The phrase 가능하면 ('if possible') is a polite way to make a request.
mistakes: Confusing 가능하다 (possible) with its opposite 불가능하다 (impossible).
Using 가능한 N to mean 'as ~ as possible'; for that, 가능한 한 + adjective is the set form.

nuance: 불가능하다 is the direct opposite of 가능하다, formed by adding 불- ('not/un-'). It means something cannot be done. In service situations it's a firm but polite way to say no, often softened with 좀 ('a bit'). For everyday 'I can't', the '-ㄹ 수 없다' pattern is also common.
mistakes: Mixing up 불가능하다 (impossible) with 가능하다 (possible) — note the 불- prefix flips the meaning.
Saying 불가능하는 N for the pre-noun form; adjectives use -ㄴ, so it's 불가능한 N.
